1.label: doc_title
1.text: Theorems of Natural Selection: Results of Price, Fisher, and Robertson

1.label: text
1.text: Is there some reorientation for the expression of natural selection that may

1.label: text
1.text: provide subtle perspective, from which we can understand our subject more deeply and

1.label: text
1.text: analyze our problems with greater ease and greater insight? My answer is ... that

1.label: text
1.text: the Price equation provides that sort of reorientation. Frank (2012, p. 1003)

1.label: text
1.text: One of the messages from Chapter 5 is that selection, even on just one or two

1.label: text
1.text: loci, can have very complex dynamics. Indeed, outside of the special case of

1.label: text
1.text: frequency-independent viability selection at a single locus, selection is not even

1.label: text
1.text: guaranteed to increase mean fitness. Nonetheless, the search for general theorems

1.label: text
1.text: (exact mathematical expressions) of selection response has motivated population

1.label: text
1.text: and quantitative geneticists for over 80 years. By shifting attention away from

1.label: text
1.text: trying to model individual allele-frequency change over a large number of loci to

1.label: text
1.text: considering the dynamics of some composite feature of these loci, such as the mean

1.label: text
1.text: of a trait, the hope was that some general statements might hold. Here we focus

1.label: text
1.text: on three classical “theorems”—Fisher’s fundamental theorem of natural selection,

1.label: text
1.text: Robertson’s secondary theorem of natural selection, and Price’s theorem—as

1.label: text
1.text: well as Lush’s breeder’s equation, summarized in Table 6.1. Ironically, these attempts

1.label: text
1.text: to bring some order to population- and quantitative-genetic theory have

1.label: text
1.text: instead resulted in a considerable amount of confusion and chaos in the literature.

1.label: text
1.text: As detailed below, the classical interpretation of Fisher's theorem, along with

1.label: text
1.text: Robertson's theorem and the breeder's equation, are all approximations (albeit often

1.label: text
1.text: good ones), and not formal mathematical theorems. In contrast, Price's general

1.label: text
1.text: expression for any type of selection response is a formal theorem, as is a special case

1.label: text
1.text: of it, the Robertson-Price identity for the within-generation response in a trait

1.label: text
1.text: due to selection. A source of confusion is that the classical view assumed by

1.label: text
1.text: most of the literature was apparently different from Fisher's own interpretation,

1.label: text
1.text: which is a formal (but not very useful) theorem. As our discussion of these various

1.label: text
1.text: "theorems," exact and otherwise, will highlight, it is the transmission of trait

1.label: text
1.text: values from parent to offspring that generally induces complications and makes the

1.label: text
1.text: theoretician's job challenging. This can be seen in Table 6.1 by simply comparing

1.label: text
1.text: the exact Robertson-Price result for within-generation change (S) with results for

1.label: text
1.text: cross-generational change $ (S + E[w\delta_z]) $. The surprising result is not that

1.label: text
1.text: these "theorems" are wrong, but rather that they often are reasonable-to-excellent

1.label: text
1.text: approximations for much of the dynamics of a trait under short-term selection.

1.label: text
1.text: Our treatment of this rather convoluted area is structured as follows. We start with

1.label: text
1.text: Price's theorem, which is a completely general description of any selection

1.label: text
1.text: response under any model of transmission. It does not rely on any explicit genetic

1.label: text
1.text: model and thus serves as an ideal platform from which to examine the other "theorems."

1.label: text
1.text: We next turn to Fisher's fundamental theorem, which has a rich and somewhat

1.label: text
1.text: checkered history, in part due to Fisher's failure to be fully explicit with his

1.label: text
1.text: definitions. An important corollary of Fisher's theorem is that, in the absence of

1.label: text
1.text: mutation, selection will drive the additive variance in fitness toward zero, and we next

1.label: text
1.text: examine some of the biological implications and misunderstandings of this result.

1.label: text
1.text: We then turn to Robertson's secondary theorem, which focuses on the selection

1.label: text
1.text: response of any arbitrary trait, not just fitness. Finally, because the breeder's

1.label: text
1.text: equation is the basic workhorse result for much of selection theory in quantitative

1.label: text
1.text: genetics (Chapters 13–20), we conclude by examining its robustness in some detail.

2.label: paragraph_title
2.text: PRICE'S GENERAL THEOREM OF SELECTION

2.label: text
2.text: The thoughtful reader might ask if there is a general, assumption-free statement

2.label: text
2.text: about selection response under any situation. There is: namely, Price's

2.label: text
2.text: theorem (Price 1970, 1972a), also referred to as the Price equation. Price's theorem

2.label: text
2.text: provides a notationally elegant way to describe any evolutionary response.

2.label: text
2.text: It makes no assumptions about the mechanism of transmission of a trait from

2.label: text
2.text: some ancestral category (such as an individual or group) to its descendants. As

2.label: text
2.text: such, it works for traits transmitted by standard genetics, epigenetics, and

2.label: text
2.text: culture, and as such has been applied to everything from the evolution of

2.label: text
2.text: languages to community structure in ecology. Recent reviews include Frank (1995,

2.label: text
2.text: 1997, 1998, 2012), Rice (2004a), Boyd and Richerson (2005), Okasha (2006), Gardner

2.label: text
2.text: (2008), Helanterä and Uller (2010), and Luque (2017), while van Veelen (2005;

2.label: text
2.text: van Veelen et al. 2012) championed a more cautious use of Price's theorem.

2.label: paragraph_title
2.text: The Life and Times of George Price

2.label: text
2.text: George Price was one of the most enigmatic figures in modern evolutionary biology

2.label: text
2.text: (Frank 1995, Schwartz 2000, and Harman 2011 all reviewed Price's life and

2.label: text
2.text: contributions). After obtaining a Ph.D. in chemistry from the University of Chicago,

2.label: text
2.text: he worked on the Manhattan Project before joining IBM as an engineer. At

2.label: text
2.text: age 44, Price quit his job and started working under Cedric Smith at University

2.label: text
2.text: College London (from 1968 to 1974). In this brief tenure, he only published four

2.label: text
2.text: solo papers and was the coauthor on two others, but in his roughly 25 total

2.label: text
2.text: pages of publications, he made three fundamental contributions to modern evolutionary

2.label: text
2.text: theory. In addition to Price's theorem, he introduced the power of game

2.label: text
2.text: theory to evolutionary biology (Maynard Smith and Price 1973), and he was the

2.label: text
2.text: first to fully grasp what Fisher had really meant by his enigmatic fundamental

2.label: text
2.text: theorem (Price 1972b). Price left academia in 1974, working as a night janitor

2.label: text
2.text: before giving away all his worldly possessions to homeless alcoholics and dying

2.label: text
2.text: by his own hand in 1975 while a squatter in one of the poorest areas of London.

3.text: Price's Theorem, $ R_{z} = \sigma(w_{i}, z_{i}) + E(w_{i} \bar{\delta}_{i}) $

3.label: text
3.text: Price’s theorem expresses the expected selection response in a trait in general terms

3.label: text
3.text: of covariances, rather than relying on any explicit model of transmission, and as such

3.label: text
3.text: is a completely general description of any evolutionary response. As succinctly

3.label: text
3.text: stated by Rice (2004a, p. 170), “it is an exact characterization of a relationship that

3.label: text
3.text: must hold between phenotype, fitness, selection, and evolution.” The key to Price’s

3.label: text
3.text: equation is to first consider the effect of selection on specific categories (measured

3.label: text
3.text: by how many descendants each leaves) and then consider how trait values may differ

3.label: text
3.text: between an ancestral category and its descendants. This is an extremely subtle shift

3.label: text
3.text: in focus, one that is easy to miss and misinterpret. However, this perspective nicely

3.label: text
3.text: decomposes the evolutionary change $ (R_{z}) $ into a selection term and a remainder

3.label: text
3.text: term due to all other forces, such as (but not limited to) imperfect transmission.

10.label: text
10.text: This simple statement from Fisher’s (1930) book (which was dictated to his wife

10.label: text

10.label: text
10.text: discussion, and sometimes heated arguments. Fisher claimed his result was exact,

10.label: text
10.text: a true theorem. Historically, the classical (and seemingly obvious) interpretation

10.label: text

10.label: text
10.text: variance in fitness, $ R_w = \sigma^2(A_w) $. Because variances are nonnegative,

10.label: text

10.label: text

10.label: text

10.label: text

10.label: text

10.label: text

10.label: text
10.text: conditions, but is often a good approximate descriptor. We first review the classical

10.label: text
10.text: interpretation, and then discuss what it appears that Fisher actually meant.

16.text: morphological characters measured in the same population or species (reviewed by Robertson

16.label: text
16.text: 1955b; Charlesworth 1987; Mousseau and Roff 1987; Roff and Mousseau 1987; also see LW

16.label: text
16.text: Figure 7.10). However, some notable exceptions are also apparent (see Charlesworth 1987).

16.label: text
16.text: The difficulty with these general surveys is knowing whether a character is highly genetically

16.label: text
16.text: correlated with lifetime fitness. Clutch size, for example, would seem to be highly

16.label: text
16.text: correlated with total fitness, but if birds with large clutch sizes have poorer survivorship,

16.label: text
16.text: the correlation with lifetime fitness may be weak. Negative genetic correlations between

16.label: text
16.text: components of fitness allow for significant additive variance in each component at

16.label: text
16.text: equilibrium, even when additive variance in total fitness is zero (Robertson 1955b; Rose 1982).

16.label: text
16.text: Unfortunately, estimates of lifetime fitness in natural populations and their correlation

16.label: text
16.text: with components of fitness (such as clutch size) are rare. One example was given by

16.label: text
16.text: Gustafsson (1986; see also Merilä and Sheldon 2000), who measured lifetime reproductive success

16.label: text
16.text: as well as the heritabilities of fitness and other characters in a closed natural population

16.label: text
16.text: of collared flycatcher birds (Ficedula albicollis) in the Baltic Sea. Lifetime

16.label: text
16.text: reproductive success had an estimated heritability that was not significantly different from

16.label: text
16.text: zero, as expected from the corollary to Fisher's theorem. Clutch size had a rather high

16.label: text
16.text: heritability, $ 0.32 \pm 0.15 $, but the estimated phenotypic correlation between clutch size

16.label: text
16.text: and total fitness was very low, $ r^2 = 0.03 $. In general, as the phenotypic correlation

16.label: text
16.text: between a trait and total fitness decreased, its heritability increased (Figure 6.3).

16.label: text
16.text: McCleery et al. (2004) also found a negative relationship between trait heritability and

16.label: text
16.text: trait-fitness phenotypic correlation in an English population of great tits (Parus major)

16.label: text
16.text: that was followed for almost 40 years. Similar findings were seen by Teplitsky et al. (2009)

16.label: text
16.text: in red-billed gulls (Larus novaehollandiae). Conversely, Schwaegerle and Levin (1991)

16.label: text
16.text: found no significant association between the heritability of a character and its phenotypic

16.label: text
16.text: correlation to fruit production (chosen as one measure of total fitness) in a wild

16.label: text
16.text: population of the plant Phlox dummondii (Figure 6.3). While the evidence is mixed, these

16.label: text
16.text: studies suggest a mild trend for characters that are phenotypically correlated with fitness

16.label: text
16.text: to have reduced heritabilities relative to other characters. One important caveat is that

16.label: text
16.text: this association is based on phenotypic, rather than genetic, correlations with fitness.

16.label: text
16.text: Under the classical view, if a trait is known to be under selection, one might be

16.label: text
16.text: tempted to assume it is still far from its genotypic equilibrium value if it shows a modest

16.label: text
16.text: to large heritability. This is false. As Example 6.6 highlights, a trait that is

16.label: text
16.text: under selection can still have a high trait additive variance even when the additive

16.label: text
16.text: genetic variance in fitness is near zero. This can happen if there is a nonlinear

16.label: text
16.text: transformation of the trait value into fitness, such as occurs with stabilizing selection.

16.label: text
16.text: More generally, Price and Schluter (1991) noted that even with a simple linear relationship

16.label: text
16.text: between a trait and fitness, it is quite likely that there may be a modest heritability

16.label: text
16.text: for the trait but a very low heritability for fitness. The following simple model

16.label: text
16.text: makes most of their main points. Assume fitness is entirely determined by a metric

17.label: text
17.text: often be misinterpreted. Suppose that locus A in Example 6.5 completely determines a character

17.label: text
17.text: under stabilizing selection. Let the genotypes AA, Aa, and aa have discrete phenotypic values

17.label: text
17.text: of z = -1, 0, and 1, respectively (so that this locus is strictly additive with respect to the

17.label: text

17.label: text

17.label: text

17.label: text

18.label: paragraph_title
18.text: Traits Correlated With Fitness Have Higher

18.label: paragraph_title
18.text: Levels of Both Additive and Residual Variance

18.label: text
18.text: While a reduced $ h^{2} $ value is often interpreted as resulting from a decrease in

18.label: text
18.text: the additive variance, it can also result from an increase in the residual variance,

18.label: text
18.text: and the argument made by Price and Schluter raises the question of whether traits that

18.label: text
18.text: are more closely associated with fitness have increased residual variances. If this

18.label: text
18.text: is the case, a simple comparison of heritabilities can be misleading (Houle 1992).

18.label: text
18.text: When comparing additive variances across traits, a standardized measure is required, and

18.label: text
18.text: a common approach is to compare coefficients of variation, the ratio of the standard

18.label: text
18.text: deviation to the mean. This led Houle (1992; see also Charlesworth 1984a) to suggest that

18.label: text
18.text: the coefficient of additive genetic variance, $ CV_A = \sigma_A / \mu $ (where $ \mu

18.label: text
18.text: $ is the trait mean) is the appropriate scale-free measure for comparing the amount of

18.label: text
18.text: additive genetic variation across traits. To distinguish this measure from the heritability,

18.label: text
18.text: Houle coined the term evolvability for $ CV_A $ (a term that has unfortunately

18.label: text
18.text: since been co-opted in a number of ill-defined ways by developmental biologists). As a

18.label: text
18.text: representative sample of Drosophila traits illustrates (Table 6.2), traits with low $ h^2

18.label: text
18.text: $ values can have very high $ CV_A $ values. Indeed, in a recent meta-analysis, Hansen

18.label: text
18.text: et al. (2011) found essentially no correlation between heritability and evolvability.

18.label: text
18.text: However, in a survey of over 800 estimates for $ CV_A $ from a variety of traits, Houle (1992) found

18.label: text
18.text: that characters assumed to be closely related to fitness (such as life-history traits) have

18.label: text
18.text: higher evolvabilities (larger $ CV_A $ values) than do traits that are more loosely associated with

18.label: text
18.text: fitness. Thus, the pattern of trait heritabilities decreasing with their correlation with fitness

18.label: text
18.text: is not due to smaller additive variances, but instead is caused by larger residual (nonadditive

18.label: text
18.text: plus environmental) variances, as quantified by the coefficient of residual variation ( $ CV_R $).

18.label: text
18.text: A study by Kruuk et al. (2000) on Scottish red deer (Cervus elaphus) offers some additional

18.label: text
18.text: insight. The authors estimated components of additive genetic, maternal, and residual

18.label: text
18.text: variances from pedigree data for this wild population (on the Isle of Rum in Scotland)

18.label: text
18.text: for five life-history and three morphological traits in addition to lifetime fitness.

18.label: text
18.text: As shown in Figure 6.4, they also found heritabilities to be negatively correlated

18.label: text
18.text: with fitness, whereas the coefficient of additive genetic variance $ CV_{A} $, was

18.label: text
18.text: positively correlated with fitness in males (but negatively correlated in females). Moreover,

18.label: text
18.text: $ CV_{A} $ values were higher for life-history traits than for morphological traits,

18.label: text
18.text: and the coefficient of residual variation $ CV_{R} $ was also positively correlated with

18.label: text
18.text: fitness. Similar patterns of both $ CV_{A} $ and $ CV_{R} $ being positively correlated

18.label: text
18.text: with fitness have been seen in the seed beetle Callosobruchus maculatus (Messina

18.label: text
18.text: 1993), in an Alberta population of bighorn sheep (Coltman et al. 2006), in the perennial

18.label: text
18.text: herb Ipomopsis aggregata (Campbell 1997), and in natural bird populations (collared

18.label: text
18.text: flycatchers by Merilä and Sheldon 2000; great tits by McCleery et al. 2004). For these

18.label: text
18.text: studies, high residual variance, not low $ \sigma_{A}^{2} $, accounts for the observed

18.label: text
18.text: lower $ h^{2} $ values for traits related to fitness. Conversely, while Teplitsky et al.

18.label: text
18.text: (2009) also observed lower heritabilities for fitness-related traits in red-billed gulls,

18.label: text
18.text: both higher residual variance and lower additive variance accounted for their trend.

18.label: text
18.text: What accounts for the higher coefficients of additive variance in traits associated with fitness?

18.label: text
18.text: The prediction of lower additive variance in fitness-related traits is based on the notion that

18.label: text
18.text: $ \sigma_{A}^{2} $ is removed by selection. However, the loss of variation is partly countered

19.label: text

19.label: text
19.text: it appears that traits that are more closely associated with fitness actually have

19.label: text
19.text: higher mutational variances (Houle et al. 1996), most likely due to a larger number

19.label: text
19.text: of loci influencing fitness (Houle 1992; Houle et al. 1996; Merilä and Sheldon 1999).

19.label: text
19.text: As with any summary metric, $ CV_A $ should be used with a little caution. Garcia-Gonzalez et

19.label: text
19.text: al. (2012) found that roughly 45% of the studies they examined used incorrect methods in

19.label: text
19.text: calculating $ CV_A $ (the most common being use of the sire variance $ \sigma_A^2 / 4 $ in

19.label: text
19.text: place of $ \sigma_A^2 $, which results in a two-fold lower estimate). A second issue is that

19.label: text
19.text: coefficients of variation should only be compared among items with the same dimensions (Lande

19.label: text
19.text: 1977c). CVs for linear measures tend to be less than those for volumetric measures. Hence,

19.label: text
19.text: something like body mass might intrinsically have a higher $ CV_A $ than some linear

19.label: text
19.text: morphological trait. These and other issues are discussed by Garcia-Gonzalez et al. (2012), who

19.label: text
19.text: provide a delta-method approximation (LW Appendix 1) for the standard error of a CV estimate.

19.label: text
19.text: A final caveat with these studies is that they examined the correlation between fitness

19.label: text
19.text: (either total fitness or one of its components) and additive variance of a trait,

19.label: text
19.text: while Fisher was concerned with the additive genetic variance of fitness itself.

19.label: text
19.text: Estimates of the additive variance in total fitness in natural populations are very

19.label: text
19.text: rare, as these require estimates of lifetime fitness (not a trivial task; see Chapter

19.label: text
19.text: 29), further compounded by the difficulty of having to obtain such estimates over a

19.label: text
19.text: set of relatives. To date, estimates of the additive variation associated with lifetime

19.label: text
19.text: reproductive success in natural populations are from vertebrates with extensive

19.label: text
19.text: known pedigrees. Kruuk et al. (2000) found no evidence for a significant heritability

19.label: text
19.text: of this trait in red deer. McCleery et al. (2004) found positive, but not significant,

19.label: text
19.text: estimates in great tits. Merilä and Sheldon (2000) found a significant additive

20.label: text
20.text: variance for females and a positive (but not significant) variance for males in

20.label: text
20.text: collared flycatchers. Teplitsky et al. (2009) found positive (but not significant)

20.label: text
20.text: variance in females and no variance in males for red-billed gulls (Larus novaehollandiae).

20.label: text
20.text: Blomquist (2010) obtained rather high ( $ \sim $0.4) estimates of heritability

20.label: text
20.text: for lifetime reproductive success in a free-ranging population of rhesus macaques

20.label: text
20.text: (Macaca mulatta) introduced in 1938 (from India) to a small island in Puerto Rico.

20.label: text
20.text: Finally, Papaix et al. (2010) obtained a very low estimate (a posterior mean of 0.02)

20.label: text
20.text: for heritability of adult survival in the wild for a population of blue tits (Cyanistes

20.label: text
20.text: caeruleus). One issue with all of these studies is the expected low power to

20.label: text
20.text: detect small amounts of variances, so negative results should be viewed cautiously.

20.label: paragraph_title
20.text: Nonadditive Genetic Variance for Traits Under Selection

20.label: text
20.text: As selection drives the additive variance in fitness toward zero, any remaining genetic

20.label: text
20.text: variance is expected to be increasingly composed of nonadditive terms. As Example 6.5

20.label: text
20.text: highlights, this nonadditive genetic variance can be considerable. Thus, characters that are

20.label: text
20.text: more closely associated with fitness are expected to have a higher fraction of nonadditive

20.label: text
20.text: variance and hence a higher residual variance. This trend can be seen in results from

20.label: text
20.text: chromosome substitution analysis (Example 6.7), which tend to show epistatic interactions

20.label: text
20.text: for life-history characters but not for morphological characters (also see LW Table 5.1).

20.label: text
20.text: Crnokrak and Roff (1995) examined roughly 340 estimates of dominance variance in

20.label: text
20.text: both life-history and morphological traits from 17 wild and 21 domestic species. In

20.label: text
20.text: the wild species, traits assumed more closely connected with fitness (life-history

20.label: text
20.text: traits) showed significantly higher dominance genetic variation (measured relative

20.label: text
20.text: to total variance) than did morphological traits. In domesticated species,

20.label: text
20.text: however, there were no significant differences in dominance genetic variance between

20.label: text
20.text: life-history and morphological traits. The presumption is that many of the

20.label: text
20.text: morphological traits examined in the domesticated species were themselves the result

20.label: text
20.text: of strong recent selection during domestication (and thus, both groups of traits

20.label: text
20.text: may have been under similar selection). This is supported by the observation that

20.label: text
20.text: morphological traits in domesticated species showed significantly higher dominance

20.label: text
20.text: variance than morphological traits in wild species. While certainly not conclusive,

20.label: text
20.text: these results are consistent with the prediction of higher dominance genetic

20.label: text
20.text: variance in traits more closely associated with fitness. Ideally, as above, the

20.label: text
20.text: comparison of the amount of dominance variance should also be examined in terms of

20.label: text
20.text: the coefficients of variation, as opposed to just the fraction of total variance.

20.label: text
20.text: Roff and Emerson (2006) presented a somewhat complementary analysis, using 90 estimates

20.label: text
20.text: for life-history traits and over 140 estimates for morphological traits from

20.label: text
20.text: line-cross data. Line-cross analysis examines the components (additive, dominance, etc.)

20.label: text
20.text: contributing to the between-line divergence, rather than the variance segregating in

20.label: text
20.text: any particular population (LW Chapter 9), and it is by no means clear if additive

20.label: text
20.text: variance being driven to zero by selection within populations translates into significant

20.label: text
20.text: nonadditive contributions to differences between line means. This important caveat

20.label: text
20.text: aside, Roff and Emerson found that the magnitude of dominance effects (relative to

20.label: text
20.text: additive effects) in line differences was much greater for life-history traits.

20.label: text
20.text: Further, epistatic effects were more often detected for life-history traits, and the ratio

20.label: text
20.text: of total nonadditive effects (dominance plus epistasis) relative to additive effects

20.label: text
20.text: for life-history traits was roughly double that for morphological traits. Finally,

20.label: text
20.text: DeRose and Roff (1999) showed that (in animals) inbreeding depression is greater

20.label: text
20.text: for life-history than morphological traits, indicating higher amounts of directional

20.label: text
20.text: dominance among segregating alleles for life-history traits (see also LW Chapter 10).

20.label: text
20.text: What accounts for the increase in residual variation for traits associated with fitness?

20.label: text
20.text: One source, as suggested by Price and Schluter (1991), is higher environmental

20.label: text
20.text: variance associated with fitness. As we have just seen, a second source is an increase

20.label: text
20.text: in nonadditive variance. While both factors likely play a role, their relative

20.label: text
20.text: importance is unknown (Merilä and Sheldon 1999). Due to the difficulty of estimating

20.label: text
20.text: nonadditive genetic variance components without special mating designs (LW Chapter 20),

20.label: text
20.text: resolving this question for natural populations is likely to prove quite difficult.

21.text: In two separate papers, Robertson (1966a, 1968) suggested that the expected response to

21.label: text
21.text: selection of any trait is a function of the covariance between the breeding value for that

21.label: text
21.text: trait and relative fitness. Robertson (1968) called this relationship the secondary

21.label: text
21.text: theorem of natural selection. While these two papers are usually jointly cited as the source

21.label: text
21.text: for this theorem, a more careful reading shows that Robertson proposed two different

21.label: text
21.text: formulae, based on whether the covariance with trait breeding value $ A_{z} $ involves

21.label: text
21.text: the phenotype (w) or the breeding value $ (A_{w}) $ of relative fitness. As a result, there

21.label: text
21.text: is confusion in the literature as to the exact form of Robertson's secondary theorem.

24.text: THE BREEDER'S EQUATION FRAMED WITHIN THE PRICE EQUATION

24.label: text
24.text: The breeder’s equation forms the backbone for much of the theory of selection

24.label: text
24.text: response in quantitative genetics (Chapters 13–20). Almost all of the theory of

24.label: text
24.text: breeding is framed around it, as is much of evolutionary quantitative genetics,

24.label: text
24.text: although Robertson’s secondary theorem has been gaining some recent traction in

24.label: text
24.text: studies in natural populations (reviewed in Chapter 20). As these results show,

24.label: text
24.text: the breeder’s equation is an approximation, with a linear parent-offspring

24.label: text
24.text: regression as a necessary, but not sufficient, condition (Example 6.1). When viewed

24.label: text
24.text: in a population-genetic framework, Example 5.12 showed that the breeder’s equation

24.label: text
24.text: is generally a fairly good approximation under weak selection on each of the

24.label: text
24.text: loci underlying a trait. Conversely, as highlighted in Example 6.3, the

24.label: text
24.text: performance of the breeder’s equation can be compromised if there are major genes,

24.label: text
24.text: especially if they display dominance. Here we conclude our discussion on theorems

24.label: text
24.text: of selection by expanding upon our earlier discussion (Equations 6.12 and 6.13)

24.label: text
24.text: to fully place the breeder’s equation into the exact Price equation framework.

24.label: text
24.text: Equation 6.12 shows that when the parent-offspring regression is linear, the

24.label: text
24.text: expression for selection response reduces to the breeder's equation plus two

24.label: text
24.text: correction terms. What can be said if we make no assumptions about the functional

24.label: text
24.text: form of this regression? The most general solution is Heywood's decomposition

24.label: text
24.text: (2005), which we build up to after introducing the partial covariance and the

24.label: text
24.text: effect of the reference population on the parent-offspring regression. Based on

24.label: text
24.text: the Price equation, Heywood's decomposition yields components with biologically

24.label: text
24.text: meaningful interpretations that go beyond simply being mathematically convenient

24.label: text
24.text: correction terms. A key point from this decomposition was foreshadowed in

24.label: text
24.text: Example 6.3—it is the parent-offspring regression after, as opposed to before,

24.label: text
24.text: selection that is more appropriate for predicting the response to selection.

27.label: text

27.label: text

27.label: text

27.label: text
